values.value: • Use the verbal assurance to tighten the path to final paperwork and payment approval. • Confirm what exactly the assurance covers: vendor preference, commercial comfort, or final internal nod. • Ask what remains before official closure. • Put dates, owners, and approval steps against the remaining tasks. • Do not relax until the verbal confidence becomes a formal commitment.
14|Yes
Buyer may say, 'We are positive, but nothing official yet.' Response: 'That is good progress. What are the last internal steps between this and a formal yes?'
Strong signal. Convert verbal comfort into a dated close plan, approval path, and clear final ask.
Low risk. Move from assurance to action.
Ask: 'Since you are comfortable moving ahead, what are the final steps and dates to get this signed off?'
Yes

• Do not assume silence means progress. • Ask directly what is still missing before they are comfortable giving verbal confidence. • Check if the gap is internal alignment, budget, risk, competition, or unresolved commercial point. • Create a close plan that earns assurance instead of waiting for it. • Move the deal from polite follow-up to buyer-led next step.
14|No assurance yet
Buyer may say, 'We need more time.' Response: 'Of course. To help properly, what would need to become clearer before you can say you are comfortable moving ahead?'
Do not keep chasing politely. Ask what is missing for a verbal yes and close that gap directly.
Risk: Proposal may be sitting without sponsor commitment.
Ask: 'What is the one thing stopping you from giving us a clear go-ahead today?'
No assurance yet

• Do not rush a proposal just because the deal feels active. • First confirm requirement clarity, buying criteria, budget direction, and buyer access. • Use the pre-proposal stage to shape expectations and reduce rework. • Send a proposal only when it will advance the deal, not merely document activity. • A well-timed proposal converts better than an early one.
14|Proposal yet to be submitted
Buyer may say, 'Send the proposal and we will review.' Response: 'Happy to. Before I do that, I want to be sure it is timed right and aligned to your actual decision criteria.'
Do not rush the proposal. First confirm problem, criteria, buyer, and budget so the proposal lands properly.
Risk: Proposal too early will weaken your position.
Say: 'Before I send numbers, I want to make sure the proposal answers the real decision points.'
Proposal yet to be submitted

• Clarify the deal stage before forecasting confidently. • Check whether the proposal has been reviewed, who has seen it, and what the current buyer position is. • Ask whether there is any informal preference already forming. • Without this clarity, the next move may be mistimed. • Re-establish where you really stand in the close path.
14|Don't know
Buyer may say, 'Let us reconnect later.' Response: 'Sure. Before that, can I confirm where we stand now so the next step is useful rather than repetitive?'
Find out whether the proposal has emotional support inside the account. Commercials without internal backing usually stall.
High risk: No clarity on buyer confidence.
Ask: 'Who is actually pushing this internally, and how do they feel about our proposal today?'
Don't know
After submitting Commercial Proposal, have we received verbal assurance from the Decision maker?
